thread.title_full: A 1982 Chicago mystery: The disappearance of 8-year-old Tricia Kellett

author: CJ Coombs
title: A 1982 Chicago mystery: The disappearance of 8-year-old Tricia Kellett
text:
3 hours ago Tricia J. Kellett. Photo by NCMEC website. Tricia J. Kellett has been missing from Chicago, Illinois (Cook County) since May 7, 1982, according to the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC). Her photo above (right) is an age-progressed likeness of how she might have looked at 48, though she would now be 53.
Notably, not all missing children are reported to the NCMEC. Some of the cases were reported to the NCMEC after this private, non-profit organization was established in 1984 . As of today, 101 missing children in Illinois, spanning from 1963 to 2026, were reported to and listed with the NCMEC.
Cases listed by the NCMEC receive direct assistance from the organization's resources, which help families and law enforcement.
About Tricia Kellett Tricia was last seen playing in the street near her home. She was only eight years old. When Tricia went missing, she was 4'0" tall and weighed about 70 pounds. She had strawberry-blonde or blonde hair and blue eyes. She had space between her front teeth.
Tricia was last seen wearing blue jeans, a blue long-sleeved sweater, and brown lace-up shoes. Additional photos of Tricia can be found on The Charley Project website. Her case was classified as a non-family abduction. Previous injuries include a broken left wrist and a fractured skull.
Tricia's parents divorced. She lived in a Chicago apartment with her mother and stepfather when she disappeared. Her father routinely visited her, and she was said to be well-known in her neighborhood.
In 1982, Tricia's mother moved out of the apartment and reportedly moved to Missouri. In 2009, her father died, but her sister was still alive at that time. Tricia is still missing.
Details One source said Tricia went outside after school to play with her friends in the street. She was waiting for her father to pick her and her brother up for the weekend. When her father arrived, Tricia couldn't be found.
Another source said Tricia was playing with puppies on a neighbor's porch and was seen getting into a car with one or two men near the corner of Leland and Malden.
The car was described as a blue 4-door 1979 Dodge that had damage on the right front door and a license plate starting with the letters "Q" and "R."
The police were called a few times during the evening of the day Tricia went missing. The authorities joined the search around 10:00 p.m. After the police obtained a description of the vehicle, Marvin Pontarelli became a suspect. The vehicle was registered to Pontarelli . His history included a background of kidnapping, sexual assault, and rape.
Pontarelli was identified as being seen with Tricia in a police lineup. He faced charges on that day for offenses relating to other children in the neighborhood. He was questioned about Tricia's case and failed a polygraph exam. Reportedly, authorities believed he may have kidnapped Tricia for sex work.
Pontarelli was picked out of a lineup by three of Tricia's friends who were between 11 and 12. They provided statements saying what Pontarelli had done to them on the day Tricia disappeared. They alleged that he took them to his apartment, gave them beer and drugs, sexually assaulted them, forced them to engage in sexual acts, and took pictures of them.
When the police searched the apartment, they found 66 items of child pornography, including photos of the three girls, guns, brass knuckles, tear gas, cattle prods, and handcuffs.
Six months later, when the victims failed to appear in court to testify against him, charges were dismissed against Pontarelli. It was reported that investigators believed the families of the victims were paid by Pontarelli so they wouldn't cooperate with the case.
In 1984, Pontarelli was living in Arizona. The police learned he wanted to photograph a young, blonde girl with a former inmate, Larry Fassler, now deceased, for blackmail purposes. Pontarelli and Fassler met in prison in California. Fassler owed Pontarelli money.
When the Chicago police found Fassler's address book, an entry dated October 1982 had Tricia's name and Chicago home address. Under her name was Pontarelli's name. Fassler contacted Arizona authorities, saying he wanted to be interviewed. He said he wrote the address book entry after he was questioned by the police about Tricia.
In 1984, Fassler contacted the authorities in Arizona and said he wanted to be interviewed. He said he'd written the address book entry after being questioned about Tricia by police. He also thought Pontarelli was the kind of person who would have been responsible for Tricia's disappearance because of his attraction to children and his history of violence.
In 1985, while Pontarelli was in custody in Arizona on unrelated charges, he was asked about Tricia and started crying. He claimed she was dead and buried on some property his family owned in Illinois and claimed Fassler was responsible for her death. Weeks later, he changed his story and speculated Fassler had taken Tricia to Mexico. However, it was Pontarelli who had previously gone to Mexico with underage girls.
If Pontarelli is responsible for Tricia's disappearance, it's been reported that her body may be buried in the foundation of Pontarelli Apartments in Chicago. At the time of Tricia's abduction, cement was being poured at the apartment complex. Pontarelli died in prison in 1994, and Fassler is also deceased.
Tricia is listed in the National Missing and Unidentified Persons System (NamUs) under case #MP2663 . NamUs is an official website of the U.S. Department of Justice. Tricia is also listed on The Doe Network under case #272DFIL . DNA is in CODIS.
Tricia has a Find-a-Grave record indicating "Burial Details Unknown."
If you have any information regarding Tricia’s disappearance or whereabouts, contact the Chicago Police Department at 1-312-747-5789 and reference agency case no. M01A8094.
You can also contact the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC) through its website at https://www.missingkids.org or its 24/7 call center at 1-800-843-5678, and reference NCMEC #601784.
The NCMEC is not automatically notified of every missing child, which might explain why the number of missing children sometimes appears low, compared to other statistics. A separate report must be made to the NCMEC, even after law enforcement enters the missing child's information into the FBI's National Crime Information Center (NCIC) database.
When a child is entered into the NCIC database, the information isn't automatically sent to the NCMEC. To activate the NCMEC's resources and support, a separate report must be submitted to them . The NCMEC provides case management, poster distribution, law enforcement assistance, and analytical support.
The number of missing U.S. children fluctuates because many runaways eventually return home. However, some cases involve endangered missing people, endangered runaways, lost or injured missing people, family abductions, non-family abductions, and, unfortunately, foul play is sometimes involved.
See NCMEC's blog contribution , "Every Missing Child Has a Story: New 2025 Statistics Highlight Hope, Recovery and Protection."
Thank you for reading and sharing. Find Tricia Kellett.
